newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Ceremony marks end of Guatemala civil war patrols.
newsitem.headline: Ceremony marks end of Guatemala civil war patrols.

text.p: One of the last units of Guatemala's notorious civil war patrols demobilized on Sunday in a symbolic ceremony marking the end of an institution widely accused of human rights abuses.

The patrols -- mandatory for all men of military age in rural areas -- were set up in the early 1980s under dictator Gen. Efrain Rios Montt to protect rural communities from leftist guerrillas of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit. But they were widely accused of human rights abuses.

The demobilization began Aug. 9 after the military decided to scrap them as a show of goodwill during peace talks to end Guatemala's 36-year civil conflict. A final peace accord is due to be signed Dec. 29 in Guatemala City.
Under bright sunshine in this mountainous western municipality, a group of shabbily dressed peasants gave up their antique M1 carbines and Mauser rifles to a military commander.
"There is no more need for rifles, but for machetes ... to work and work in peace," Col. Augusto de Leon Cabrera of the nearby military base at the town of Huehuetenango told the patrollers.
Many Maya women, dressed in their colourful traditional costumes, ignored the ceremony in favour of market day.
At its height in 1982-83, the patrols involved 1.3 million men. The law that created them was repealed on Thursday.

The programme, which according to the military is supposed to decommission some 13,000 firearms and demobilize nearly 300,000, ends with Sunday's event and a similar ceremony on Monday in the nearby municipality of Chiantla.
But doubts persisted over the accuracy of the military figures in the absence of any independent verification.

"There has been no international supervision of the process so it is hard to get details about how many arms have been collected," said John Bevan, coordinator for the U.N. observer mission Minugua in Huehuetenango.
"No one apart from the army knows how many were given out in the first place. Nobody is checking where the arms are coming from or how many there are."

Patrols in the region were accused of massacres on several occasions in the early 1980s, though not on the scale seen elsewhere in the country during Rios Montt's scorched-earth campaign against the rebels.
Some 140,000 people have died or "disappeared" during Latin America's longest-running guerrilla war.
